Q23.text: I use Twitter mainly to follow conversations around science communication and public engagement -- things like how scientists discuss uncertainty, or ongoing debates around replication and public trust in research. It's less about promoting my own work and more about staying connected to broader discussions of how research is perceived (and often misperceived) by non-specialist audiences.

Q29.text: Social media -- Twitter in particular -- has been genuinely useful for tracking conversations at the edges of my field, things that haven't yet made it into journals or formal proceedings. It's less efficient for finding primary literature (I still rely on databases for that), but as a way of sensing which questions are gaining traction or which methodological debates are live, it's honestly pretty hard to replicate with conventional tools.

Q37.text: Sharing is probably where I feel most ambivalent, honestly. Twitter makes it easy to put work in front of people who wouldn't normally encounter it through journal alerts or institutional channels, which matters if you care about research reaching beyond specialist audiences. That said, the incentive structure tends to reward punchy takes over nuanced findings -- I've seen careful work flattened into a headline-friendly tweet that doesn't really serve the underlying research well.

Q43.text: Promotion feels like a slightly different question from sharing -- there's a more deliberate, almost strategic quality to it that I'm not entirely comfortable with. Twitter can amplify work that deserves wider attention, but the norms around self-promotion in academia make it feel awkward at times. I tend to share things when they connect to a broader public conversation rather than as a way of building my own profile -- which I guess is a selective way of engaging with the promotion function.

Q47.text: Networking is probably where platforms like Twitter deliver most consistently for me -- not in a formal "let's collaborate on a project" sense, but in terms of building a kind of ambient awareness of what other researchers are thinking and working on. I've had genuinely useful exchanges with people I'd never have encountered through conference circuits alone, particularly around science communication practice. That said, it tends toward the conversational end of the collaboration spectrum; actual research partnerships still seem to need more structured channels to get off the ground.

Q63.text: Better integration between journal platforms and social sharing would help -- right now the friction involved in turning a paper into something shareable outside specialist circles is entirely on the author. If publishers provided plain-language summaries or structured abstracts alongside technical ones, that would make it much easier to communicate findings accurately on Twitter without either losing nuance or losing the audience. I think there's also an underused opportunity around threading DOI-linked content into broader public conversations, though I'm not sure how you'd do that without it feeling like corporate noise.

Q65.text: I'd add that we're still in an early, slightly awkward phase where researchers are navigating norms that havent really settled -- what counts as appropriate self-promotion, how much to simplify, whether engagement metrics actually mean anything useful. I remain cautiously optimistic that platforms like Twitter can serve a genuine public-good function around science literacy, but that probably depends on the research community developing clearer shared expectations rather than just individual trial and error.

Science and research literacy is poor for much of the general public, so it's beneficial to learn this way.

Q23.text: Following scientists and labs I admire, honestly -- great way to keep up with work before it even hits journals. I also use it to engage with non-academic audiences about my research, which feels really important to me as someone who thinks science communication is one of the most undervalued parts of academic life.

Q29.text: Honestly, I think it's massively underused for this -- the ability to follow a lab's progress in real time and ask questions directly to researchers you'd never get to meet otherwise is kind of incredible. Twitter especially has changed how I approach my own research development. Why wait for a conference when you can just have that conversation now?

Q37.text: Sharing is honestly where I think social media shines most. Posting a preprint or a figure to Twitter and getting feedback within hours -- that's something journals just can't replicate. I do wish more researchers treated their accounts as a proper communication channel rather than an afterthought, but the potential is there and its exciting to see it growing.

Q43.text: Promotion is maybe where I feel most conflicted -- I love the idea of getting your work in front of people who'd never find it through traditional channels, and Twitter especially can do that really well. But there's a fine line between sharing and self-promotion that I think some researchers cross, and it can feel a bit uncomfortable. That said, for someone like me who cares deeply about public engagement, the ability to promote work directly to a curious non-academic audience feels genuinely exciting

Q47.text: Networking is honestly where I see the most untapped potential -- connecting with researchers at other institutions who work on adjacent problems, without needing to wait for a conference or a formal introduction. I've had conversations on Twitter that genuinely shaped how I think about my own work, and that still kind of amazes me. The geographic barriers just dissolve in a way that feels really significant for early-career researchers especially.

Q63.text: Better integration between journal pages and social sharing would be a huge help -- right now it often feels like publishers treat the paper as the endpoint, but honestly the conversation that happens after publication is just as valuable. Clearer licensing around sharing figures and preprints on Twitter would make a real difference too; I'm never quite sure what I'm allowed to post and it makes me hesitant. I guess just making it easier to share content without worrying about accidentally violating terms would go a long way

Q65.text: I just want to say that I genuinely think we're at an inflection point with how researchers communicate -- Twitter especially has the potential to reshape how science moves from lab to public in real time. I'm still early in my career but I already cant imagine doing research without it. It'd be great to see institutions and publishers lean into that rather than treat it as a distraction

Q23.text: I follow researchers in my field to keep track of new work -- not always through formal channels since access to journal is a real problem where I am. Facebook groups have been useful for hearing about conference and sometimes finding papers shared informally (which for serious researchers in the Global South is honestly quite important). I also use it to follow environmental and policy debates that connects to my research area.

Q29.text: Social media can be useful resource for research but it wasn't really built with serious researchers in mind, especially those of us outside the major hubs. I find it helpful for following developments in my field (though you have to wade through a lot of noise to find anything relevant), but the lack of integration with actual academic content is real limitation -- platforms like Facebook are built for engagement, not for knowledge building. An scholar-oriented equivalent would honestly be more valuable

Q37.text: Sharing is where I think the potential is clearest, but also where the frustration is most acute. Platforms like Facebook make it easy to circulate a link, but if that link leads to a paywalled journal, serious researchers outside well-funded institutions are just hitting a wall again. Informally shared PDFs in Facebook groups help, but that's a workaround not a solution -- what we really need is platforms built around open, accessible content rather than ones that bolt sharing onto an advertising infrastructure.

Q43.text: Promotion is useful in theory but I find it somewhat harder to evaluate than sharing -- when I post something or share a link on Facebook, I have no real sense of whether it reached anyone who matters academically. For researchers like me without an already-established following, promotion through general social media feels like shouting in a noisy room. A scholar-specific platform where serious researchers are actually concentrated would make promotion far more meaningful, rather than competing with posts about travel and family photos for attention.

Q47.text: Networking is probably where I see the most genuine value, honestly -- I've made a few connections through Facebook and ResearchGate with researchers working on similar questions, and that's been useful in a way that wouldn't have happened through formal channels alone. But the same problem keeps coming up: general platforms scatter serious researchers among so much other content that finding the right people is more luck than design. For those of us in the Global South, where conference travel is expensive and institutional networks are thinner, a well-structured scholar platform for networking could make a real difference -- not just another LinkedIn but something actually built around research communities.

Q63.text: The most obvious thing would be making content more openly accessible -- publishers investing in open access infrastructure that actually works for researchers in lower-income countries, not just token gesture. Beyond that, it would help if publishers built better social sharing tools into their own platforms, not just a "share to Facebook" button but something that let serious researchers circulate and annotate work within a research-focused context. Some publishers are moving in this direction honestly, but the paywalls remain the biggest obstacle to any of this being meaningful

Q65.text: I suppose what I'd want to leave here is that this isn't really about being against social media -- its that the infrastructure we have was built for different purposes than serious research, and researchers in places like mine feel that gap most acutely. The connections I've made have been genuinely valuable, but always despite the platform rather than because of it. If publishers, universities, and developers took this seriously there is real potential -- but it needs to be built with us in mind, not adapted from something designed to sell advertisements

Q37.text: Sharing is a mixed bag for me. Q43.text: Promotion is where it gets really uncomfortable for me. Q47.text: Networking is where it gets genuinely interesting, actually. I HAVE found people — real thinkers, cross-disciplinary, willing to question what most researchers treat as settled — and social media is how that happened. Not ResearchGate, not Academia.edu, not any of the formal platforms built to connect people doing the same kind of experiment-on-subjects work I find unconscionable. those platforms connect the establishment to itself. But the informal spaces? yes, there's real connection possible there. The "collaborations" I value are more like... mutual recognition, shared frameworks, people who see what I see across fields. Formal co-authorship with the mainstream research community isnt something I'm pursuing, so in that narrow sense the SCN value is limited for me.

Q63.text: Honestly, the thing publishers could do that would actually matter to me is provide better mechanisms for flagging research that raises serious ethical concerns — not post-publication corrections about methodology, but REAL ethical review, visible to readers. Right now the formal channels treat that as settled before publication. That would change how I engage with professional content on these platforms entirely. other than that, I dont really use the publisher-affiliated tools enough to have strong opinions on the interface or features.

Q65.text: I suppose the main thing I'd add is that I exist in an uncomfortable in-between space with all of this. I see the value — I've LEARNED from these tools, connected with people I genuinely respect, built up a knowledge base that spans fields most researchers would never cross. and I did it without harming anyone. But the professional infrastructure around scholarly communication — the SCNs, the publisher networks, the whole apparatus — is mostly built to circulate work I find morally indefensible, and I cant pretend otherwise. So my use stays informal, selective, on my own terms. That's probably not what this survey is hoping to hear but it's the honest answer.

Q29.text: ResearchGate is useful to some extent because it automatically aggregates your publications and citations without much effort on my part, which I do appreciate, but I am not really convinced it supports actual research activity in deeper sense -- it feels more like passive monitoring tool than something that actively helps develop work or find new directions, and honestly the rest of social media is so fragmented that I dont know where to even begin with most of it

Q43.text: Promotion is where I feel most uncertain honestly, because ResearchGate makes your papers visible automatically which is convenient but I am not sure that really counts as active promotion -- it feels more like passive availability rather than deliberately reaching new audiences. Q47.text: Networking is something I find difficult to evaluate honestly -- ResearchGate does show you who is following your work and occasionally I receive messages from researchers asking about specific papers, which is useful kind of serendipitous contact, but I wouldn't say I am actively networking through it in any meaningful way. Q23.text: I occasionally use these platforms to track emerging debates in my field, though I'm cautious about treating anything I find there as reliable without independent verification -- they can serve as a kind of early-warning system, I suppose, if nothing more.

Q29.text: There is some value in being able to quickly identify what topics are attracting attention, but I remain sceptical of platforms that mix rigorous findings with speculative content without meaningful distinction. If these tools could somehow surface only peer-reviewed work, they might genuinely support research development -- rather than simply amplifying noise.

Q37.text: Sharing professional content through these platforms does have genuine potential, particularly for reaching audiences who lack journal access. That said, I worry about findings being stripped of their context as they circulate -- a carefully qualified result can look very different once summarised in a post or a tweet. I'd be more confident in these tools if stronger norms existed around linking to full, open-access versions of research rather than just the headline

Q43.text: Promotion is perhaps where I feel most ambivalent -- there is an inherent tension between advocating for one's own work and maintaining the detachment that research demands. These platforms can reach broader audiences, honestly, but I worry that the incentives around visibility might encourage researchers to overstate findings or quietly downplay uncertainty.

Q47.text: Networking is perhaps where I see the most genuine promise -- identifying researchers working on adjacent problems can be surprisingly useful, and I have found occasional value in that. That said, I'm not convinced online connections translate easily into sustained collaboration; they seem to function more as a discovery layer than as real working infrastructure, if that makes sense.

Q63.text: Better integration between journal platforms and SCN tools would help -- if publishers made it genuinely easy to share open-access versions of articles directly from the publication page, that would address much of my concern about decontextualised sharing. I think what I'd find most useful is something like a verified, non-profit sharing layer that publishers collectively maintained, where findings could circulate with their caveats intact rather than stripped down to a headline. At the moment it feels like publishers treat social media as a promotional afterthought rather than a serious infrastructure question.

Q65.text: My overall sense is that these platforms occupy an uneasy space between genuine utility and structural risk -- I use them selectively, but I'm not sure that selective use is a sustainable position as they become more central to how research circulates. What I'd really want, and what doesn't yet exist, is a shared infrastructure built around research integrity rather than engagement metrics; something non-profit, peer-governed, and designed to keep findings in context. Until something like that exists, I'll keep treating social media as a useful but unreliable signal rather than a foundation for anything serious.

This is the most serious issue of research at this time.

Google tracks use, so searches become more and more limited.  People not registered for universities with certain databases have NO access to some of the most rigorously conducted research.  Somehow, these two need to merge so that valid research is available to all and nonsense is clearly marked as nonsense.

Q23.text: Occasionally I use Twitter to follow conference hashtags when I can't attend in person, which is honestly one of more useful things these platforms offer -- you get a reasonable sense of what was discussed without the time and cost of travel. I also track citations through ResearchGate, though I'm not sure that counts as active use so much as passive monitoring.

Q29.text: There's genuine value in being able to follow developments in adjacent fields through platforms like Twitter or ResearchGate — things you might miss if you relied only on journal alerts. But I find the signal-to-noise ratio pretty poor, and the time investment required to extract that value is rarely acknowledged. it can feel like the expectation is that you'll simply absorb this on top of everything else, without any structural recognition that browsing social media is a legitimate form of professional development rather than recreational distraction.

Q37.text: Sharing content -- posting preprints, linking to publications -- is probably where I see the clearest case for these platforms. getting a paper in front of people who might actually read it, beyond whoever happens to browse the journal, seems like a reasonable goal. That said, I'm genuinely uncertain how much of this translates to anything measurable, and there's something uncomfortable about the performative aspect of it -- the sense that you're not just sharing work but curating an image of productivity. I do it, but without much confidence that the time cost is justified

Q43.text: There's obvious overlap with the sharing question, and honestly I'm not sure I can cleanly distinguish the two in practice. Promotion feels more deliberate -- more about visibility and brand than just making work accessible -- and that's where my ambivalence deepens. The academic reward structure still runs on publications and citations, not on how well you've curated your online presence, so investing significant time in self-promotion feels structurally misaligned with what actually gets evaluated. I do use Twitter to push out links when something is published, but I do it with a kind of unease, like I'm performing a role that the system asks of me without actually valuing it.

Q47.text: Networking is probably the area where I feel most genuinely conflicted. There have been moments -- a Twitter exchange that led to a useful follow-up email, a ResearchGate message that opened into something like a real collaboration -- that I wouldn't have expected to trace back to social media. But those feel like exceptions, and I'm wary of building a practice around rare wins. Most of what passes for networking online is pretty superficial and doesnt translate to meaningful collaboration; the actual work of building research relationships still happens through conferences, emails, and institutional proximity. I use these platforms for this, but I wouldn't overstate their role.

Q63.text: The main thing I'd find useful is better curation rather than more volume -- publisher newsletters and blog updates tend to add to the information overload problem rather than help with it. If publishers could offer more selective, field-specific digests rather than broad promotional emails, that would actually be something. I'd also find it helpful if there were clearer guidance on what sharing is permitted under different access arrangements, since I'm sometimes uncertain whether I can post a preprint link or a manuscript version without inadvertently violating something. Mostly though I suspect publishers have limited influence over the structural problems I find most frustrating -- the mismatch between what they encourage and what institutions actually reward

Q65.text: I suppose the thread running through most of my answers is that social media use for professional purposes feels structurally orphaned -- the system asks you to do it, colleagues do it, institutions gesture toward it as part of your "research profile," but none of that translates into how you're actually evaluated or resourced. it's not that these platforms are without value, clearly they're not, but the gap between the informal expectation and the formal reward structure creates a kind of background friction that I don't think gets acknowledged enough. I'd find it genuinely useful if there were more honest institutional conversation about what this work actually costs and whether the returns justify it, rather than treating social media engagement as something researchers should simply absorb into already overstretched schedules.

Q23.text: I use it mainly to follow public health debates and to occasionally push back on misinformation circulating in my field. The issue is not the platform itself but what people do with it -- and researchers have responsibility to engage rather than leave the space to non-experts. I monitor certain discussions more than I contribute, honestly.

Q29.text: As resource for staying current, social media has real value -- I've come across debates and preprints I would never have found through standard journal alerts. The problem is signal-to-noise, especially in public health topics where misleading content spreads faster than corrections. Used carefully it supports research awareness, but it requires active filtering and honestly that costs time

Q37.text: Sharing is probably where social media works best, at least for reaching audiences beyond your immediate academic circle. I've had colleagues in public health tell me a single tweet got their findings to journalists and policymakers faster than any press release. the downside is that complex findings get stripped down to a headline, which can distort the message -- especially when the topic touches something like vaccine safety where even a partial reading is dangerous.

Q43.text: Promotion is honestly where I feel most ambivalent. On one hand, visibility matters -- a paper that no one reads has no impact, and social media does expand reach considerably. But promotion logic pushes you toward simplification, toward the catchy framing rather than the accurate one, and in public health that tension is not trivial. I've seen well-intentioned posts backfire because the headline attracted the wrong reading.

Q47.text: Networking is probably the area where I have fewest complaints, tbh. For connecting with researchers outside your immediate institution -- especially across disciplines or in countries where you'd otherwise never overlap -- it genuinely helps. I've made a couple of useful connections through Twitter exchanges that would not have happened at conferences I couldn't attend. the caveat is that it favours the already-visible, and those of us working on less fashionable topics get less traction.

Q63.text: One thing that would help is better plain-language summaries built into the paper itself -- something accurate and citable that a researcher can share without having to write their own version and risk oversimplifying. If publishers produced short lay abstracts designed for social media use, it would reduce that temptation considerably. Misrepresentation problem partly starts with having no good shareable version of the actual findings.

Q65.text: The broader point I'd add is that misinformation on social media wont be fixed by individual researchers doing better -- it needs a collective response, and the scholarly community has honestly been slow to develop norms around this. Institutions and publishers both have a role, but right now most of the burden falls on individual judgement, which is not a stable solution

Q65.label: Q65
Q65.text: I think it should be encouraged more. The power of social media to disseminate information is too great to be ignored. Often false/incorrectly understood content is promoted as truth and this has created recently too many issues. One example: major measles outbreak in Romania, cause by disseminating false information about vaccine safety over social media and TV

Q23.text: I use social media mainly to promote conference events that I help organise -- reaching audiences who wouldnt normally come across traditional academic announcements. I also advise graduate students on appropriate (and inappropriate) uses of these platforms, which comes up more often than you might expect. ResearchGate too, honestly, mostly for accessing papers that are otherwise paywalled.

Q29.text: ResearchGate has been genuinely useful for accessing literature that would otherwise require going through institutional library channels, so there is real practical value there. for broader research development though, I'm honestly less convinced -- it depends heavily on your discipline and whether your community has actually adopted these tools in any meaningful way. I tend to advise my students to be selective rather than assuming a platform will accelerate their work just because others use it.

Q37.text: There's real value in being able to share conference announcements and papers directly to a wider audience -- particularly people outside the usual scholarly circuits. That said, I'm not convinced the engagement always justifies the effort involved. I've found Facebook useful for event promotion, less so for substantive content sharing, and the reach varies so much by field that its hard to generalise.

Q43.text: There is obvious overlap with sharing here, though promotion feels slightly more intentional -- you're actively trying to build visibility rather than just distributing. I've had reasonable results using Facebook and Twitter to push conference announcements and my own work to people outside my immediate network, but I remain cautious about the time investment. Honestly it can become a bit of a performance rather than genuine engagement, and I advise my students to be mindful of that distinction.

Q47.text: Networking via social media has its uses -- I've made initial contact with researchers at other institutions through Twitter, and ResearchGate has occasionally surfaced collaboration opportunities I wouldnt have found otherwise. Real collaboration still tends to happen through conferences and direct email though; social media is more of a starting point than a sustained channel. The signal-to-noise ratio can honestly make it more work than its worth, depending on how active your particular community is on these platforms.

Q63.text: Better integration between publisher platforms and ResearchGate or similar SCNs would help -- at the moment the process of making papers discoverable outside the journal's own ecosystem feels piecemeal. I'd like to see publishers take a more proactive role in sharing metadata and DOI links in formats that play nicely with these platforms, rather than leaving that work to individual authors. Honestly, making open access more straightforward would do more for discoverability than any social media feature.

Q65.text: The main thing I'd add is that the risk side of this often gets underplayed -- particularly for early career researchers who may not yet understand how a poorly judged post can follow them professionally. I spend more time warning students about this than encouraging use, which probably reflects my overall stance: these tools have genuine utility, but they require the same judgement you'd apply to any professional communication. There isnt a neat formula for it, and I think that's what publishers and platform developers tend to underestimate.

Q23.text: I occasionally use ResearchGate to locate preprint or author-accepted versions of papers that would otherwise be inaccessible behind paywalls — this is driven by necessity rather than any enthusiasm for the platform itself. The inability to access published work without an institutional subscription is a serious impediment to research, and social networks have partly filled that gap by allowing researchers to share their own outputs, however informally. I also sometimes encounter references to retracted or significantly corrected papers through Twitter alerts, which helps me avoid inadvertently citing compromised work. Honestly though, I find the overall landscape of scholarly social media poorly organised and not well suited to these tasks.

Q29.text: Social media and SCNs offer a partial workaround for a problem that publishers should have solved themselves — namely, universal access to the scientific literature. The fact that researchers rely on informal sharing via ResearchGate or Academia.edu to obtain papers their institutions cannot afford to license is, honestly, an indictment of the current publishing model rather than a vindication of social media. As a tool for supporting research activity more broadly, I find these platforms inconsistent and difficult to navigate; the signal-to-noise ratio is poor, and the information is not reliably curated. We are patching a systemic failure with improvised tools, and that is not a sustainable or adequate solution.

Q37.text: Sharing professional content via social media or SCNs has become a practical necessity for many researchers, but I'm not sure this represents genuine progress. The primary reason researchers post their work on these platforms is that the official published versions are locked behind paywalls that most readers cannot access — so what we call "sharing" is largely compensating for a failure of the formal publishing infrastructure. There are also real concerns about version control: readers cannot always tell whether they are reading a final peer-reviewed article or an earlier draft with uncorrected errors, and that ambiguity compromises the integrity of the literature. The platforms themselves do little to clarify this. This is a problem.

Q43.text: The promotion of professional content via social media has become something researchers feel obligated to engage in, rather than something they do because it is genuinely effective. The pressure to maintain a visible online profile — posting preprints, sharing citations, accumulating followers — has been largely created by the failure of traditional publishing to make research reliably discoverable and accessible. I find this expectation troubling: it shifts the burden of dissemination onto individual researchers while doing little to address the structural problem of access. Metrics derived from social media engagement are also increasingly used in informal assessments of research impact, yet they are poorly standardised and easily gamed. Conflating visibility with quality is, honestly, not progress.

Q47.text: Networking via social media and SCNs is, honestly, probably the area where these platforms come closest to fulfilling a genuine function — direct contact between researchers has always been valuable, and platforms like ResearchGate or Twitter do occasionally facilitate connections that might not have occurred through formal channels. That said, I find the networking dynamic on these platforms increasingly performative: follower counts and engagement metrics create incentives for visibility rather than meaningful intellectual exchange. Genuine collaboration tends to emerge from shared work and mutual trust, not from social media interactions. The platforms themselves benefit from engagement regardless of its quality, which means their design actively works against the kind of slow, careful collaboration that research actually requires. That tension is not incidental.

Q63.text: The most obvious thing publishers could do is stop treating access as a revenue lever and make the published literature universally available — that would immediately reduce researchers' dependence on informal sharing platforms as a workaround. If the record of science were openly accessible, much of what we currently use social media and SCNs for would be unnecessary. Beyond that, publishers could invest in better metadata standards and persistent identifiers so that when papers are shared informally, readers can reliably establish whether they are looking at a final version or a preprint. The current situation, where version ambiguity is endemic, is partly a publisher failure of infrastructure. honestly, the simplest improvement they could make is to not require improvement workarounds in the first place.

Q65.text: The overarching point I would make is that the current role of social media and SCNs in scholarly communication reflects a fundamental failure of the publishing system rather than an organic development. Researchers have been compelled to adopt these tools not because they are well-suited to scholarly work, but because the formal infrastructure has failed to deliver on its basic obligations — open, reliable access to the scientific record. I am not convinced that further adoption of these platforms will improve matters; they introduce new problems around version integrity, engagement metrics, and the blurring of informal and formal communication. The solution lies in fixing the infrastructure, not in normalising the workarounds. honestly, that distinction matters.

For those who have been publishing for a long time and are trying to return to the workforce, the danger of limited access to journals is authors often cite a reference when they have only read the abstract. Abstracts are not always representative of the entire paper, so incomplete information enters the literature stream. This is a problem.

Q23.text: I use Facebook and Instagram primarily for science communication to a general audience, which I see as a genuinely important but often undervalued part of being a researcher -- the gap between what scientists know and what the public understands is pretty significant and I feel some responsibility for that. I dont really use these platforms for professional peer communication though, I keep that strictly to email and private channels because I find the professional networking platforms like ResearchGate and LinkedIn a bit hollow for actual scientific exchange.

Q29.text: For actual research support I think the platforms marketed specifically for researchers -- ResearchGate, Academia.edu -- dont deliver as much as they promise, and I've found direct email contact with colleagues far more productive for genuine scientific exchange. That said, maintaining a public social media presence does feed back into my research in indirect ways, because engaging with non-specialist audiences forces me to articulate what actually matters in my work and to examine assumptions I've never had to make explicit before, which is honestly a kind of informal peer review in itself.

Q37.text: For sharing with a general audience Facebook works pretty well for me, I can post about recent papers or findings in a way that reaches people who would never read a journal article and the response -- even just a comment or a share -- tells me something about which aspects of the science resonate with non-specialists. For sharing with peers though I dont use social media at all, I send papers directly by email because ResearchGate feels more like self-promotion than actual scientific exchange.

Q43.text: There's a distinction I keep coming back to between promoting work to a general audience and promoting it within your professional community, and for the former Facebook actually does something useful -- people share content and it reaches beyond your immediate followers in a way that a journal article simply cant. For the latter I dont think social media adds much, the researchers whose attention you actually want are better reached through conferences or direct contact than through platforms that feel designed more for self-branding than genuine scientific exchange.

Q47.text: For networking and collaboration with other researchers I honestly dont find social media useful at all -- the interactions I've had on ResearchGate or LinkedIn have felt pretty superficial, more like people collecting connections than actually exchanging ideas. Real collaboration happens for me through email, through conferences, and through the kind of slow-building relationships that come from sustained scientific exchange rather than a follow button. I guess if anything my public outreach on Facebook has occasionally led to researchers reaching out to me, but that feels more like a side effect than a feature of the platform.

Q63.text: The thing that would make the biggest practical difference for me is if publishers made it easier to share findings in a form that non-specialists can actually engage with -- a plain-language summary attached to every paper, something I could link to from Facebook without feeling like Im sending people behind a paywall or into a wall of jargon. Open access is part of this but its not enough on its own if the content is still written for specialists, and right now I end up doing that translation work myself which is fine but not really scalable.

Q65.text: I suppose the main thing Id want to leave anyone reading this with is that the value of social media for researchers isnt uniform -- it depends entirely on what youre trying to do and who youre trying to reach, and conflating public outreach with professional networking leads to platforms that do neither particularly well. For me the distinction is clear and I dont think that will change, but I do worry that pressure to be visible on all platforms simultaneously is pulling researchers away from the actual work, which is a cost that rarely gets acknowledged.

For real professional content that I want to share with colleagues, I generally just use email or private messaging, since I dont like the linkedin or researchgate platforms very much.

Q23.text: I use these mainly to keep track of broader debates in my field -- policy discussions around open access, for instance, or emerging critiques of publication practices. I'm cautious though about treating anything I encounter there as authoritative; quality of information varies considerably and not all users exercise appropriate discernment.

Q29.text: There is real value in being able to monitor developments across disciplines without waiting for formal publication cycles. however, I am sceptical that most researchers have developed the critical habits needed to filter signal from noise on these platforms -- how many follow a field primarily through social feeds and mistake that for comprehensive coverage? Usefulness ultimately depends on the discernment the individual brings to it.

Q37.text: Sharing content through these platforms has obvious reach advantages -- a preprint or finding can circulate quite quickly across communities. the concern, however, is governance: there's little quality control over what gets amplified, and the promotional logic of these platforms tends to reward visibility over substance, which I'm not sure serves scholarly communication well.

Q43.text: Promotion sits even closer to marketing logic than sharing does, and I find myself more ambivalent here. There is a difference between making work genuinely discoverable and performing visibility for its own sake -- and these platforms tend to blur that line considerably. whether that ultimately serves research communities or primarily individual careers is, I think, an open question worth taking seriously.

Q47.text: Networking is probably where I see the clearest genuine value -- trusted collaborators are easier to stay in contact with, and occasionally you do encounter someone through a platform whose work turns out to be genuinely relevant. I'm cautious, however, about mistaking broad connectivity for meaningful collaboration; having many connections is not the same thing as having productive ones, and I think the platforms encourage a kind of shallow engagement that can crowd out the deeper interactions that actually advance research.

Q63.text: Better metadata and clear versioning on shared content would help -- knowing whether something has been peer reviewed when I encounter it in a feed matters considerably. more broadly, publishers could do more to support open access in ways that dont simply shift costs elsewhere; that would at least reduce some of the governance tensions that make these platforms harder to rely on.

Q65.text: I suppose the overarching point I'd make is that these platforms have genuine utility as peripheral awareness tools, but the research community has been somewhat uncritical in its adoption of them. the pressures around visibility and engagement are real, and they shape behaviour in ways that aren't always aligned with good scholarly practice -- that tension seems underexplored in how publishers and institutions currently think about social media guidance.
